title: The Temperature Dependence of ΔH
lead: Tables give enthalpies at one temperature, usually 25 °C. Carrying an enthalpy change or a reaction enthalpy to another temperature takes the heat capacity, as a constant over a small range or as an empirical fit over a broad one.
exercise_notes: The book prints no exercises here; the question and its solution were written by AI. The numeric answer accepts a 2% tolerance.

exercises.prompt: Find the enthalpy change of 1 mol of N2(g) heated at constant pressure from 298 K to 400 K, using the parameters for N2(g) in Table 19.13.1.

answer.hint: Put $a = 28.58$, $b = 3.77\times10^{-3}$ and $c = -5.0\times10^{4}$ into Equation 19.13.5 term by term.
answer.solution: With $\kTone = 298$ K and $\kTtwo = 400$ K, the three terms of Equation 19.13.5 are $a(\kTtwo - \kTone) = 28.58 \times 102 = 2915.2$ J, $\tfrac{b}{2}(\kTtwo^2 - \kTone^2) = 1.885\times10^{-3} \times 71196 = 134.2$ J and $-c\left(\tfrac{1}{\kTtwo} - \tfrac{1}{\kTone}\right) = 5.0\times10^{4} \times (-8.557\times10^{-4}) = -42.8$ J. Their sum is $\kDeltaH = 3006.6$ J $\approx 3.01$ kJ. The constant term carries almost all of it: over this range $\kCpheat$ of N2 stays close to $a$.

footnotes.html: Equation 19.13.1 prints the lower limit as $T_2$; the integral runs from $T_1$ to $T_2$.
The temperature dependence of $C_p$ is Equation 19.13.3.

The table gives $a = 22.13$ J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> for Pb(s), which is the value behind the first term, 1770.4 J/mol. The other two terms are 293.5 J/mol and 79.7 J/mol, not 295.5 and 470.5, so $\Delta H = 2143.6$ J/mol rather than 2534.4 J/mol.
The integrand should read $\Delta C_p\, dT$.

The −46.11 kJ/mol is per mole of NH<sub>3</sub>, but the reaction as written forms two moles and $\Delta C_p$ below is taken for the whole reaction. For the reaction as written, $\Delta H(298\,K) = -92.22$ kJ and $\Delta H(373\,K) = -95.63$ kJ; per mole of NH<sub>3</sub>, the enthalpy of formation at 100 °C is −47.81 kJ/mol, not −49.5 kJ/mol.

steps.cap: Each term integrates by the power rule, $\int \kT^n\, d\kT = \kT^{n+1}/(n+1)$, which turns $c/\kT^2$ into $-c/\kT$.
